Neonatal Cape Verde giant skinks emerge from parchment-shelled eggs at a remarkably small size, with a snout to vent length of approximately 6.95 centimeters [Lb = approximately 6.95 centimeters] at birth. Field studies of gravid females collected from the arid islands of the Cape Verde archipelago have provided initial data on reproductive output. Under stable thermal conditions typical of the species' active season, 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is inferred from a combination of litter size and reproductive frequency. Females typically produce two young per litter [N_R_i = two young per litter], though reproductive events are infrequent, occurring only once every two years under natural conditions [F_R_i = reproductive events are infrequent, occurring only once every two years under natural conditions]. This slow reproductive pace, yielding a maximum of only one litter biennially, is consistent with the life-history strategy of a large-bodied skink facing resource-limited island environments. The neonates themselves are precocial, emerging fully formed and capable of independent locomotion almost immediately after hatching, though they remain dependent on yolk reserves for a brief period before commencing active foraging on small invertebrates.

The ontogenetic trajectory of Chioninia coctei reveals pronounced sexual dimorphism in ultimate body size, with males attaining a significantly larger ultimate snout to vent length of 35 centimeters [Li = 35 centimeters] compared to females, which reach a maximum SVL of only 31.5 centimeters [Li = 31.5 centimeters]. This size disparity is accompanied by differences in the timing of sexual maturation between the sexes. Males reach puberty at a younger age of approximately 5 years since birth [tp = approximately 5 years since birth], whereas females require a longer developmental period, attaining sexual maturity at roughly 6 years since birth [tp = roughly 6 years since birth] at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. These maturation schedules, measured at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], reflect the energetic demands of achieving a larger body size in males versus the allocation of resources toward reproduction in females. The prolonged period required to reach sexual maturity in both sexes is characteristic of a species operating under a slow life-history pace, likely constrained by low and unpredictable resource availability in their native xeric habitats.

Adult body mass in this species reaches a substantial ultimate wet weight of 858 grams [Wwi = 858 grams], placing Chioninia coctei among the larger scincid lizards globally. This impressive adult size, estimated from morphometric relationships with egg dimensions, contrasts sharply with the modest wet weight at birth of 9.22 grams [Wwb = 9.22 grams]. The approximately ninety-three-fold increase in body mass from birth to adulthood underscores a prolonged growth phase that may span several years, as individuals allocate significant resources to skeletal and muscular development before diverting energy toward reproduction. The size at which puberty is attained, as indicated by snout to vent length, is approximately 23 centimeters [Lp = approximately 23 centimeters] for both sexes. This threshold represents a critical developmental milestone, after which individuals begin the transition from juvenile growth to reproductive investment. The substantial body mass required to initiate reproduction likely contributes to the delayed maturation schedules observed in this species, as individuals must accumulate sufficient energy reserves to support gestation and parturition.

Embryonic development in this species proceeds over an extended incubation period, with an age at birth of approximately 160 days [ab = approximately 160 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This prolonged incubation duration, comparable to that reported for the related Australian sleepy lizard Tiliqua rugosa, reflects the slow metabolic rates typical of large-bodied scincids adapted to temperate and subtropical climates. The resulting hatchlings then embark on a lengthy developmental journey, with maximum recorded longevity under favorable conditions reaching approximately 16 years [am = approximately 16 years] at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This lifespan was estimated under laboratory conditions at the same ambient temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], though wild individuals may experience shorter lifespans due to predation pressures and environmental stochasticity. The extended incubation and considerable lifespan together place Chioninia coctei at the slow end of the reptile life-history continuum, prioritizing long-term survival over rapid reproduction. The leathery-shelled eggs are typically deposited in sheltered crevices or beneath rocks, where the stable thermal microenvironment approximates the 25 °C [T = 25 °C] conditions used in captive studies.

Comparative analysis of reproductive parameters across related skink taxa reveals that the Cape Verde giant skink's strategy is one of extreme iteroparity. The combination of a small litter size of two offspring [N_R_i = litter size of two offspring] and an exceptionally low reproductive frequency of one litter every two years [F_R_i = one litter every two years] yields a maximum reproductive rate of only 0.5 offspring per year [Ri = 0.5 offspring per year] when calculated under the standard thermal conditions of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This allocation pattern is consistent with the island syndrome, where endemic reptiles often exhibit reduced fecundity and increased longevity compared to mainland relatives. The maximum reproductive rate, derived from the product of litter size and frequency, suggests that a reproductively active female could produce approximately one offspring per 365 days over her lifetime, though actual output is likely lower due to intermittent breeding and resource limitation. The physiological trade-off between producing a small number of well-provisioned offspring and maintaining the large adult body mass of up to 858 grams [Wwi = up to 858 grams] appears to govern the entire life history of this species. Understanding these parameters is critical for conservation planning, as the species is currently classified as extinct in the wild and persists only in captive breeding populations.
